# Joy Laking

Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking is a Canadian visual artist renowned for her paintings of Nova Scotia's natural landscapes and towns , . For over five decades, she has worked primarily with watercolour, oil, and acrylics, developing a distinctive style characterized by strong composition and an expressive use of color and form , . Her professional practice began in Nova Scotia in 1972, and her work has been exhibited nationally and internationally, earning her significant recognition within the Canadian art community , , . Laking is also recognized for her role as an advocate for realism in art, co-founding the organization PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia) to support contemporary realist painters in the province , . Her body of work includes numerous solo exhibitions at prominent galleries, public commissions, and the publication of a book chronicling her artistic journey , . Through her art and community leadership, Laking has made a substantial contribution to the cultural identity of Nova Scotia.

## Biographical Background

Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking was born in 1950 in Owen Sound, Ontario, Canada , . She pursued higher education at the University of Guelph, where she graduated in 1972 with a Bachelor of Arts degree, majoring in Fine Art , , . Following her graduation, she moved to Nova Scotia, where she has lived and worked as a professional artist since that year , , . She currently resides in Portapique, near Great Village, Colchester County, or Bass River, in Nova Scotia, where she maintains her home and studio gallery , , . The studio is located on a Bay of Fundy salt marsh, providing a constant source of inspiration for her work .

Laking’s artistic vocation was deeply influenced by her family background. Her mother was a professional painter, and her father crafted marionettes and toy trains, creating a household saturated with creative energy . Her childhood home reportedly had art drawers in every room, reflecting a pervasive environment of artistic exploration from an early age . This nurturing atmosphere likely played a crucial role in fostering her passion for art. A pivotal and profoundly influential event in her life was the death of her mother from breast cancer around 1972, shortly after she completed her university studies , . This personal tragedy is described as having a significant impact on her career path, shaping the emotional depth and dedication evident in her subsequent work. In 1972, the same year she graduated and lost her mother, she married Jim Wyatt; together they have a son and a daughter , . Her husband has been involved in the operation of the Joy Laking Gallery, which she runs near Bass River, Nova Scotia , . Despite living with asthma and muscular dystrophy, she continues to paint professionally .

## Artistic Practice and Philosophy

Joy Laking’s artistic practice is defined by a dual methodology that combines spontaneous outdoor creation with meticulous studio refinement, resulting in a unique and cohesive body of work , . A central element of her process is plein-air painting, where she completes entire watercolour works directly on location . This technique allows her to capture the immediacy of a moment, focusing intensely on the transient effects of tides and lighting over a period of four to seven hours . These on-location studies serve as the foundation for her larger studio paintings . While working outdoors, she often prioritizes capturing the essence of the scene through direct observation, later translating these impressions into more developed compositions in her studio.

Her studio process is one of contemplation and development, often evolving over several weeks . Paintings may be derived from on-location studies, photographs, or even physical objects like flowers brought indoors . This extended period of reflection allows her to refine her initial sketches into complex works that reflect a deep engagement with their subject matter. Laking herself describes her artistic philosophy as one where all her paintings are 'singing'—a phrase that encapsulates her pursuit of a distinct artistic voice and aesthetic harmony . This concept is rooted in her technical priorities, which include a strong compositional structure, a rich tonal range, and an expressive application of materials . In her watercolours, she emphasizes the expressive potential of the paper white, while in her oils and acrylics, she focuses on creating rich color palettes . This commitment to both structural integrity and expressive quality is what defines her mature style and distinguishes her work within the contemporary realist movement.

Beyond her individual artistic output, Laking engages with her community through her art in meaningful ways. One notable example is the installation of her watercolour painting *Chairs at High Tide* in the healing garden at North Cumberland Health Care Centre in Pugwash, Nova Scotia . The artwork became the twentieth piece in the Pugwash Open Air Gallery, an initiative that displays large-scale reproductions of local art in outdoor public spaces to promote both artistic excellence and community wellness . This act demonstrates her belief in the power of art to contribute positively to public life and well-being, extending the reach and purpose of her work beyond traditional gallery settings.

## Professional Career and Major Works

Joy Laking’s professional career, spanning over fifty years, is marked by a consistent focus on Nova Scotia as her primary subject and a series of significant exhibitions that have solidified her reputation as a leading regional artist , . Her career highlights include numerous solo exhibitions at prominent institutions across Canada, national tours of her work, and public commissions that demonstrate widespread recognition of her talent. A chronological overview of her major professional milestones illustrates the trajectory of her success and the breadth of her artistic output.

| Year | Milestone |
| :--- | :--- |
| 1982 | First solo exhibition titled *Flowers of Nova Scotia* at Mount Saint Vincent Art Gallery. |
| 1984 | Created cover art for the MTT provincial phone book; held a 50-painting exhibition at Royal Botanical Gardens, Burlington., |
| 1985 | Held first solo exhibition in New Brunswick at Owens Art Gallery, Mount Allison University. |
| 1988 | Opened the Joy Laking Gallery in Portapique, Nova Scotia. |
| 1989 | Presented a 40-piece watercolour exhibition at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia. |
| 1989-1990 | The Art Gallery of Nova Scotia exhibition toured for one year., , |
| 2006 | A pink grapefruit painting was featured on a Canadian postage stamp for fundraising by the Jewish General Hospital. |
| 2016 | Served as an artist-in-residence at Port Bickerton Lighthouse., |
| 2017 | Painted in the gardens of Claude Monet, France. |
| 2021 | Held two exhibitions at Fraser Art Gallery in Tatamagouche, Nova Scotia. |

The opening of her own gallery in Portapique in 1988 provided her with a dedicated space to showcase her work and connect directly with the public . The gallery remains open by appointment as of 2025, continuing to serve as a hub for her art . Her residency at Port Bickerton Lighthouse in 2016 and her trip to paint in Claude Monet’s gardens in 2017 highlight her continued engagement with both iconic Canadian locations and international artistic heritage , . The tour of her 1989 exhibition at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia is particularly noteworthy, as it indicates that her work was considered significant enough for a wider audience across the province, showcasing her ability to produce a body of work with broad appeal and critical resonance , , . Furthermore, her work has transcended the gallery circuit, appearing on official provincial materials and charitable commemorative stamps, underscoring her status as a celebrated figure in Nova Scotia culture .

## Advocacy and Community Engagement

Joy Laking's influence extends beyond her individual artistic production to encompass active advocacy and leadership within the broader art community, particularly concerning the promotion of realism as a vital and legitimate artistic practice in Nova Scotia . Recognizing the challenges faced by contemporary realist painters, including geographic isolation and a perceived lack of institutional support, she took a proactive role in shaping the regional art scene . In 2009, she co-founded PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia), a collective of realist painters dedicated to supporting its members and raising the profile of realism in a province with a long-standing tradition of representational art , . By creating this organization, Laking and her colleagues sought to build a stronger network for collaboration, mentorship, and mutual promotion, thereby addressing some of the systemic barriers facing artists working outside of major urban centers.

Her commitment to advancing the cause of realism was not limited to organizational founding but also included curatorial and public advocacy. In 2014, she served as a key organizer for the 'Realism Revisited' exhibition at the Dalhousie Art Gallery . The exhibition, which ran from January 17 to March 9, was curated by Tom Smart and co-piloted by Peter Dykhuis, director-curator of the gallery, and was held to mark the gallery’s 60th anniversary . This high-profile show provided a significant platform to re-examine and celebrate the relevance of realism in contemporary art. Beyond organizing exhibitions, Laking has publicly advocated for greater institutional recognition of realism, citing its historical dismissal in many public galleries as a challenge that needed to be addressed . This vocal stance positions her as a thought leader who uses her standing within the art community to fight for the legitimacy and visibility of her chosen artistic style.

This dedication to community and advocacy is further reflected in her institutional affiliations and service. She is an elected member of the Society of Canadian Artists, a peer-selected honor that signifies recognition by her fellow professionals , . Additionally, she served two terms on the Board of Governors for the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia, demonstrating a deep commitment to the stewardship and development of the province's premier art institution . Her involvement in bringing exhibitions like 'Across the Surface' to Truro also highlights her role in enriching the cultural offerings of various communities within Nova Scotia . Through these multifaceted efforts—as a founder, curator, advocate, and board member—Joy Laking has consistently worked to strengthen the artistic ecosystem in which she operates, ensuring greater opportunities and recognition for realist artists in the region.

## Broader Contributions and Personal Resilience

Joy Laking's contributions to public discourse and her response to profound community trauma reveal a multifaceted artist engaged with social issues and capable of expressing deep human emotion through her work. Beyond her celebrated landscape paintings, she authored and published the educational play *Invisible Prisons*, a monologue-based work that addresses the serious issue of domestic abuse . Released in two versions in 2013 and 2014, the play was made freely available to schools, community groups, and police departments through the website www.invisibleprisons.com . This initiative demonstrates her desire to use her creative talents for social good, aiming to raise awareness and provide resources to combat a pervasive social problem. Her authorship adds a significant dimension to her profile, establishing her not only as a visual artist but also as a writer and advocate for vulnerable populations.

This capacity for empathy and social commentary is poignantly illustrated by her personal experience during the April 18–19, 2020, mass shooting in Nova Scotia, one of Canada's deadliest acts of violence . The tragedy struck close to home for Laking, as three of her friends were killed. Lisa McCully, a schoolteacher, was killed in her home, while Joanne Thomas and John Zahl were killed at their home, which was subsequently burned to the ground as part of one of 16 crime scenes investigated . The loss of these friends left a deep and lasting impact on Laking. She publicly described experiencing severe depression and a profound sense of loss of artistic inspiration immediately following the event . This candid sharing of her grief marks a significant shift in her emotional and creative life, highlighting the vulnerability of artists and the profound effect that community trauma can have on their work. It underscores the intimate connection between her life experiences and her artistic expression, showing that her art is not created in a vacuum but is deeply intertwined with the joys, sorrows, and resilience of her community.

## Awards, Honors, and Legacy

Joy Laking's contributions to the arts and her community have been formally recognized through several prestigious awards and honors, cementing her legacy as a respected and influential figure in Nova Scotia's cultural landscape. Among her most notable accolades are the Halifax Progress Club Woman of Excellence Award, which she received in 2009, and the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Medal, awarded to her in 2012 , , . The Queen's Diamond Jubilee Medal was a special Canadian award issued to commemorate the 60th anniversary of Queen Elizabeth II's accession to the throne, recognizing individuals for exceptional achievement and service to their community and country . Recipients are selected through a rigorous process involving federal, provincial, and territorial governments, indicating that Laking's contributions were deemed outstanding on a significant scale . In addition to these honors, she was also awarded the Cobequid Arts Council Lifetime Achievement Award, further testifying to her sustained impact on the arts in her region .

It is important to note that while Joy Laking has received numerous honors, she has not yet been appointed to the Order of Nova Scotia, the province's highest civilian honour , , , . The Order of Nova Scotia, established in June 2001, recognizes individuals who have made an outstanding contribution to the prosperity, growth, or general good of the province , . Official announcements of recipients for 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024 do not include her name among the honorees, a fact that has been explicitly confirmed by multiple sources , , , . As of December 2024, a total of 126 individuals had been invested into the order . The absence of her name from these lists provides a clear and accurate record of her honors, distinguishing between the high level of recognition she has already achieved and the distinction of being a member of the province's highest order.

To conclude, Joy Laking's legacy is multifaceted. She is celebrated as a masterful painter whose depictions of Nova Scotia's landscapes have become iconic representations of the province's character , . Her long and prolific career, supported by a robust exhibition history and public commissions, has established her as a cornerstone of the regional art scene , . Equally significant is her role as a community builder and advocate who worked to elevate the profile of realism and support her fellow artists through the founding of PLANS and her service on the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia's board , . Her foray into writing with the socially conscious play *Invisible Prisons* demonstrates a commitment to using her voice for broader societal benefit . Finally, her public articulation of grief following the 2020 mass shooting reveals a deep connection to her community and a capacity for profound emotional expression, adding a layer of human resilience to her story . Collectively, these contributions affirm her status as a vital and enduring cultural figure in Nova Scotia and Canada.

#### Artist Statement

As a painter, I focus on strong compositions that utilizes the full range of tonal value. During my many years of full-time painting, coupled with my en plein air practice, I have honed my ability to capture the beauty of Nova Scotia and the world. While I paint in watercolour, oil and acrylic, I delight in all things creative.

[Visit the Artist's Website](http://www.joylakinggallery.com/) 

![Image 5: Joy-PhotoJuly-2016-1024x1024.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5fb5571e24edaf5d8fe80cc1/1609451294113-3J8COEGS1NIXCQS647YO/Joy-PhotoJuly-2016-1024x1024.jpg)

#### About the Artist

Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking was born in Owen Sound, Ontario in 1950. The daughter of an artist, she graduated from the University of Guelph with a major in Fine Art in 1972. Since that time, she has lived and painted professionally in Nova Scotia. She currently resides in Portapique, Nova Scotia where she paints from her home and studio.

Laking has exhibited provincially, nationally and internationally including a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia, which was subsequently toured for year. She is an elected member of the Society of Canadian Artists, a founding member of PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia) and she has served two terms on the Board of Governors for the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia.

In 2009, Joy received the Halifax Progress Club Woman of Excellence Award and in 2012, she received the Queens Diamond Jubilee Metal. She is the 2016 recipient of the Port Bickerton artist residency.

[![Image 1: Painter Joy Laking is one of the organizer’s of a new realist art show set for 2014 at the Dalhousie Art Gallery.](https://robertpopefoundation.com/wp-content/themes/striking/includes/timthumb.php?src=https://robertpopefoundation.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/article1.jpg&w=718&zc=1&q=100)](https://robertpopefoundation.com/2013/01/nova-scotia-artists-get-real-about-realism-organize-painting-show/# "Painter Joy Laking is one of the organizer’s of a new realist art show set for 2014 at the Dalhousie Art Gallery.")![Image 2](https://robertpopefoundation.com/wp-content/themes/striking/images/image_shadow.png)Painter Joy Laking is one of the organizer’s of a new realist art show set for 2014 at the Dalhousie Art Gallery.

Concerned about a lack of public gallery attention, a group of Nova Scotia realist painters is behind a contemporary realist painting exhibit to be held from Jan. 17 to March 9, 2014, at the Dalhousie Art Gallery.

The exhibit, to have about 50 paintings by 10 to 20 artists, will be curated by Canadian art writer-curator Tom Smart with Peter Dykhuis, director-curator of the gallery, acting as “co-pilot.”

Deadline for the call for applications is March 1.

“I really sense a lot of public galleries don’t have any respect for realism,” says Joy Laking, one of the exhibit’s organizers.

“Realism is somewhat dismissed.”

The realist painter started PLANS, or Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia, in 2009 as a group of eight realists that included Tom Forrestall, Ed Huner, Paul Hannon, Gordon MacDonald, Shelley Mitchell, Susan Paterson and Steven Rhude.

“It was partly selfish,” Laking says in a phone interview from her studio in Portaupique, near Great Village, Colchester County.

“Living where I do, I don’t see other artists very often.”

She also wanted to raise the profile of realist art in a province that has a long history of realism.

Although she is a board member of the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia, she was unable to persuade the gallery to take on this idea.

“I was trying to think of a way to increase membership and visitation and the profile of realism, but that didn’t work out.”

Dykhuis remembers the day the PLANS members knocked on his door.

He had just finished programming a Montreal exhibit by Quebec realist painter Pierre Dorion for the Dalhousie Art Gallery, to run this March 15 to May 12. “Ironically, the day I signed the contract for the Pierre Dorion show, the whole PLANS group showed up with this proposal,” Dykhuis says.

“I was already in the state of mind of reinvestigating the idea of what realism is.”

The timing is good because 2014 marks the 60th anniversary of the gallery and realism is “a subject that has spanned” its history.

PLANS has received partial funding from the Robert Pope Foundation to hire an administrator, Sue MacIsaac, and curator Smart, former director of the McMichael Canadian Art Collection.

Smart is noted for his award-winning, critical biographies, catalogues and books on Canadian artists, including painters Alex Colville, Mary Pratt, Forrestall, Miller Brittain and Fred Ross.

Smart will make studio visits in the spring and summer.

“I want to be his co-pilot,” says Dykhuis.

“We’re trying to reinvestigate this subject. I don’t think it’s healthy to have one monolithic point of view.

“I want to set a high bar in terms of what realism is about and what does it mean with its heritage in Nova Scotia.”

Realism goes back to 1850 internationally. It was a key strain in mid-to-late 20th century Atlantic Canadian art through Christopher and Mary Pratt, Colville and Forrestall.

Today, says Dykhuis, several young artists at NSCAD University are pursuing representational and realistic work.

“Some of my colleagues are raising their eyebrows, but I’m going, ‘I want to go down the rabbit hole.’

“I think it’s time to go back to what does it mean to make a painted image that is supposedly realistic in a digital age.”

The term realism is “fraught” and “that will be part of the clarification.”

“The PLANS people realize just because they are kick-starting this doesn’t mean they get into the exhibition,” says Dykhuis. “We could get hundreds of applications because these questions haven’t been asked in possibly decades.”

Laking is pleased with the gallery.

“We couldn’t have asked for a more beautiful space.”

The exhibit, which is unprecedented, will be “what Nova Scotia realists need,” she says.

“It’s very exciting.”

Art and healing come together in Pugwash
========================================

Image

![Image 2: Artist Joy Laking stands with her husband, Jim, and daughter, Danica, in front of her painting Chairs at High Tide during a celebration in the Healing Garden at North Cumberland Health Care Centre.](https://www.nshealth.ca/sites/default/files/styles/masonry/public/2025-10/2.png?itok=pzIpjL-r)

North Cumberland Community Health Foundation recently welcomed patients, families, staff and guests to the healing garden at North Cumberland Health Care Centre (NCHCC) in Pugwash for a special unveiling.

_Chairs at High Tide_, a watercolour by renowned Nova Scotia artist Joy Laking, is the newest piece to join the space where many come seeking rest and reflection. With its cool blues and iconic Adirondack chairs, the artwork was chosen in collaboration with staff to reflect the values of peace, care and healing.

“The cool blue colours soothe the soul,” says Louise Cloutier, co-founder of the Pugwash Open Air Gallery. “It feels like we are transported to another location. When you are in hospital with the weight of the world, art like this allows you to escape and breathe a little easier.”

The celebration brought together Joy, her family, members of the Pugwash Open Air Gallery Committee, staff, and foundation members. Guests shared tea, coffee and cupcakes in the garden, surrounded by stories and laughter.

For Joy, who has been painting Nova Scotia landscapes for more than 50 years, the chance to contribute to a space designed for healing carried special meaning. “I have been capturing the beauty of Nova Scotia for decades,” she says. “Whenever possible I paint on location. It is an exhilarating challenge to set out, find a subject, and complete an entire painting in four to seven hours. These paintings are loose, spontaneous and depict the tides, the lighting, and the moment. It’s my hope that this work helps bring a sense of calm and connection to everyone who visits.”

The installation is the 20th artwork added to the Pugwash Open Air Gallery, a cultural project under the umbrella of Communities in Bloom which encourages the development of artistic excellence and stimulates awareness of and interest in visual arts. The initiative brings large-scale reproductions of local art to outdoor spaces, making them accessible to everyone, while highlighting the region’s creative talent.

“The concept of an open-air gallery would not be possible without the support of our community, who host reproductions or original art in buildings, making it accessible to all,” says Louise. “Thank you to NCHCC for welcoming us when we proposed hanging an art reproduction in the garden. As advocates of wellness, it’s clear they value the role that art plays in healing.”

The healing garden itself continues to grow with the support of the North Cumberland Community Health Foundation, which has also added Adirondack chairs and a gazebo for patients, families and staff to enjoy. Together, these touches of art and nature help create an environment where healing is not just about medicine, but also about moments of reflection, beauty and community.

_Photo of artist Joy Laking with her husband, Jim, and daughter, Danica, in front of her painting Chairs at High Tide during a celebration in the Healing Garden at North Cumberland Health Care Centre._

Joy Laking is “Our Joy” because she lives near Bass River, is a life member of the Truro Art Society, is always contributing and giving back to the community and, when she travels abroad (helping in places such as Bolivia and India), she’s a great ambassador/representative of us.

She is always forthright, honest and caring, wearing her heart on her sleeve and is a joy to be around. She has such love for our community and I know she was instrumental in bringing the upcoming Across the Surface Exhibition here to Truro.

Laking has been a professional artist living and working in Nova Scotia since 1972. She has had national solo exhibitions, as well as one at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia. She has received the Woman of Excellence Award as well as the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Medal. She is a founding member of PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia) and an elected member of the Society of Canadian Artists.

On the eve of her works showing at the McCarthy Gallery as part of the PLANS show, she sat down to tell us something of her work.

**Q. How did you start making art?**

**A.** My mom was a professional artist, so I grew up in a home that had art drawers in every room. When I was in high school, I discovered my friends didn’t all have art drawers.

“Where do they keep their art supplies?” I thought.

My mother always told me to be anything except an artist. From first-hand experience, she knew the artist’s life was difficult. She thought I should be a teacher or a nurse; some job with a reliable income.

I also learned something else from my mother’s early death from breast cancer. When I was little, she put her art on the back burner in order to be a perfect 1950s wife and mother. She still painted every week, not just everyday. She always intended to get back to her art full-time once my brother and sister and I were independent. She didn’t live long enough for that.

As a result, when my own children were young, I still managed to paint everyday for at least six hours. I used to get up at 5 a.m. and get into the studio to get four uninterrupted hours in before the children’s day began. During that time, I would be in the creative mindset long enough to plan and start paintings. In the afternoon, I would paint for a further two hours, (essentially just filling in and painting) while the children napped or played in a play space just outside the studio. They knew that during those hours, I was available for emergencies, but not for snacks or fun or play.

**Q. What is your background?**

**A.** I graduated with a major in Fine Art in 1972 from the University of Guelph. I don’t think I really learned much that was practical at university, but I loved the experience and it certainly broadened my horizons because I appreciated all that art could do and be.

**Q. Which artist has inspired you most?**

**A.** I’ve always been inspired by the tenacity and pigheadedness of Emily Carr. Everyone thought she was crazy, but she believed in herself enough to carry on doing what she did.  It was such a marvelous eye-opener for her when she discovered the group of seven and found a few kindred spirits.

**Q. Where can we find your work?**

**A.** I have a website at [www.joylakinggallery.com](http://www.joylakinggallery.com/). I have the Joy Laking Gallery Facebook page and my husband, Jim Wyatt, helps me operate my own art gallery near Bass River, Nova Scotia. In the summer, we’re open everyday and the rest of the year we’re open by chance or by appointment (902-647-2816).

Who is Joy?
-----------

Joy loves to paint. For forty-four years she has painted Nova Scotia and captured her view of the world on watercolour paper and in oil and acrylics. She is inspired by all of  the beauty that is Nova Scotia.

Joy's studio paintings are developed from on location paintings, photos and actual objects and flowers. Sometimes an idea is thought about for a number of years before a painting is started. The actual painting may take several weeks. In all cases the reality in the painting is Joy's. She happily changes or moves objects within a painting.  Strong compositions and a wide range of tonal values are a constant in all of Joy’s paintings.  Her watercolours make full use of the white of the paper and her oils and acrylics are full of rich colours. All of Joy's paintings "sing".

In addition to her studio paintings and when ever possible Joy paints on location. It is an exhilarating challenge to set out, find a subject and complete an entire painting in four to seven hours. These paintings are loose, spontaneous and depict the tides, the lighting and the moment. Besides painting on location throughout the Maritimes, Joy also paints around the world, most recently in India, Ghana, Italy and Portugal.

The first time I ever saw a Joy Laking painting was many years back when scrolling through the internet.   There before me was her image of – Joan’s Chairs.  I immediately looked up the artist and found her website.  I have been a fan of hers ever since. This painting is included in her book _The Painted Province_ and it was wonderful to see it again here.

![Image 1](https://miramichireader.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/number-three.png)

Joan’s Chairs

I was immediately transported back to my childhood rural Nova Scotia home.  Joy has a way of evoking the exact feeling to transported me back to a simpler time growing up in rural Nova Scotia.  In my “mind’s eye” I see my mother and her best friend sitting on just such a porch, laughing and chatting, as my friend and I head down to the beach that stretched out below the home of my mother’s best friend.  Joy sees with her heart and all the feeling comes out through her brush.  Here was that image again in Joy’s much-anticipated book – _The Painted Province_

Recently I had the distinct pleasure of opening this long-awaited book and learning more about Joy, her painting and her process.  Sitting beside my living room window glancing out an October snowy wonderland, I delightedly distracted myself by turning page after page of paintings by one of my favourite Maritime artists and visiting my home province from afar.  The artist’s name is appropriate – she brought me much joy!

Many things make up this book.  Joy’s “word pictures” on every other page are her way of capturing the beauty of a place with words.  She does this so effectively that I want to weep with her insight into the places she paints.  It is so obvious she feels deeply and her ability to portray this in words and paintings is exceptional.

I especially loved her “word picture” about her process – setting out in her car to paint.  “I just drive along waiting for something to call out to me.  When something catches my eye, I am usually beyond it.  I turn my car (Malorie) around and go back and take photos.  At this point, I am assessing the spot.  I continue doing this until I hear a clear loud “Paint Me.”

In the introduction she explains that the stories in this book are meant only to make you smile.  I promise you they will.

My husband joined in the delight in this book.  He too was enraptured with each turn of the page.  Joy’s rendering of Starry Night at the Library had him buzzing with excitement.  Different from most of the other paintings in the book it is Joy’s nod to Vincent Van Gogh’s Starry Starry Night which is one of my husband’s favorite.

![Image 2](https://miramichireader.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/number-one.png)

Starry Night at the Library

Seeing the historic street of my hometown, Shelburne, was one of the many highlights of the book for me.

![Image 3](https://miramichireader.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/number-two.png)

Shelburne

This book is more than a coffee table book or a visual book of beautiful artistry.  This book is a travel companion.  In fact, Joy Laking thinks this book should not sit on your shelf or reside on your coffee table.  She wants you to take it along in your car and says the best place to keep it is your glove compartment.  To that end she has included a map of painted province areas and the GPS co-ordinates for 39 of the paintings and would love for you to enter those co-ordinates and visit the exact spots where she painted them.

On our return to Nova Scotia my husband and I will pack this book and using the GPS will indeed visit _The Painted Province of Joy Laking_.

Whether you are a Nova Scotian, born and raised or planning to visit the province, you should carry along this book – _The Painted Province_.  Sitting in your chair turning the pages or carrying it along with you as you travel you will find much “joy” in discovering parts of the province I love so much.  I know you will fall in love with it too.

Her paintings have been exhibited nationally and internationally. **Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking** (born 1950) is a Canadian visual artist and author based in [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia "Nova Scotia"), especially known for her [watercolour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") depictions of Nova Scotian scenes. Born to an artistic family in [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), Laking painted with her mother at a young age before earning a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in 1972, subsequently moving to Nova Scotia where she went on to earn a national reputation. Laking opened a gallery in 1988 at her [Portapique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portapique "Portapique") home to display her work, which remains open by appointment as of 2025.

Laking's paintings are characterized by [representational realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_/(arts/) "Realism (arts)"), and have been displayed in Nova Scotia, [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick "New Brunswick"), Ontario, and [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") – including exhibitions at the [Art Gallery of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Gallery_of_Nova_Scotia "Art Gallery of Nova Scotia") and the [Royal Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Botanical_Gardens_/(Ontario/) "Royal Botanical Gardens (Ontario)") in [Burlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_Ontario "Burlington, Ontario"). Her writings include _Invisible Prisons_, a [play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_/(theatre/) "Play (theatre)") performed in Nova Scotia and [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)"); and the books _Colours in Winter_ and _The Painted Province_, published in 2019 and 2020, respectively. Laking's work has earned her awards such as the Lifetime Achievement Award from the Cobequid Arts Council and the [Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II_Diamond_Jubilee_Medal "Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal").

Early life and education
------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joy_Laking&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")\]

Laking was born in 1950 in [Owen Sound, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Sound "Owen Sound"), to an artistic family. Her mother was a professional painter, and her father crafted [marionettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marionette "Marionette") and [toy trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy_train "Toy train"). As a child, Laking frequently accompanied her mother on trips to the [Georgian Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_Bay "Georgian Bay") to paint the scenery of the area. While enjoying these trips, she initially felt inadequate due to the difference in quality between her artwork and her mother's.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201126-2) Laking attended secondary school at [Owen Sound Collegiate and Vocational Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Sound_Collegiate_and_Vocational_Institute "Owen Sound Collegiate and Vocational Institute") until graduating in 1969, predicting in a Grade 8 writing assignment that she would be making a living as an artist within ten years.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Sun_Times1996aThe_Sun_Times1996b-3) She graduated from the [University of Guelph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Guelph "University of Guelph") with a Bachelor of Arts in 1972, marrying the same year, and subsequently moving to Nova Scotia with her husband.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201129%E2%80%9330Visual_Arts_Nova_Scotia2014-4) Around the time she graduated, her mother died of breast cancer, which would have a profound impact on her artistic career as her mother inspired her to become an artist.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201125%E2%80%9326PNI_Atlantic_News2014a-5)

Between 1980 and 1985, Laking and her husband had three children: Kelsey, Danica, and Yolande.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201130-6)

[![Image 3: Entrance of the Joy Laking Gallery](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Joy_Laking_Gallery_entrance.jpg/250px-Joy_Laking_Gallery_entrance.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joy_Laking_Gallery_entrance.jpg)

[![Image 4: Sign for the Joy Laking Gallery by the road](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Joy_Laking_Gallery_sign.jpg/250px-Joy_Laking_Gallery_sign.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joy_Laking_Gallery_sign.jpg)

The Joy Laking Gallery opened in the late 1980s in [Portapique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portapique "Portapique")

Following her move to Nova Scotia in 1972, Laking settled in [Bass River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_River,_Nova_Scotia "Bass River, Nova Scotia") and began her art career.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201130-6) In the early 1980s, she illustrated two children's books: _The Brook and the Woodcutter_ and _The Man Who Couldn't Stop Sneezing_ by [Gary Saunders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Saunders "Gary Saunders"). While she enjoyed the illustration work, she considered the payment to be inadequate, and had to seek other opportunities. She subsequently released a set of calendars featuring her paintings.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201133-7) Laking went on to hold her first solo [exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_exhibition "Art exhibition") titled _Flowers of Nova Scotia_ at the [Mount Saint Vincent Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Saint_Vincent_University#Art_Gallery "Mount Saint Vincent University") in 1982 and she began to earn a national reputation.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Sun_Times1986The_Griffin2015-8) In 1984, her work was chosen to be featured on the cover of the [MTT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_Telegraph_and_Telephone_Company "Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Company") provincial phone book,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2016a-9) and 50 of her watercolour paintings were put on display at the [Royal Botanical Gardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Botanical_Gardens_/(Ontario/) "Royal Botanical Gardens (Ontario)") in [Burlington, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington,_Ontario "Burlington, Ontario").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Hamilton_Spectator1984-10) In 1985, Laking held her first [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick "New Brunswick") solo exhibition at the Owens Art Gallery at [Mount Allison University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Allison_University "Mount Allison University").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Times-Transcript1985-11) In the late 1980s, Laking and her husband built the Joy Laking Gallery at their [Portapique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portapique "Portapique") home to display her work,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201134-12) opening the gallery in 1988.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Sun_Times1988-13) Her paintings have also been sold at private galleries in [Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax,_Nova_Scotia "Halifax, Nova Scotia") and [Hamilton, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Ontario "Hamilton, Ontario"). Between 1982 and 1992, Laking participated in six group exhibitions and held nine solo exhibitions,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201134%E2%80%9337-14) including a 40-piece [watercolour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") exhibition at the [Art Gallery of Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Gallery_of_Nova_Scotia "Art Gallery of Nova Scotia") in 1989, followed by a regional tour until May 1990.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Sun_Times1989Joy_Laking_CV2024-15) A collection of her paintings featuring summer and winter scenes was displayed at the Royal Botanical Gardens in 1990.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Hamilton_Spectator1990-16)

In 2006, a painting of a pink grapefruit by Laking was chosen to be featured on a postage stamp, as part of a campaign to raise funds for the [Jewish General Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_General_Hospital "Jewish General Hospital") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Gazette2006-17) In 2007, after overcoming a serious health issue and inspired by travelling, Laking underwent what she referred to as an "explosion of creativity", branching out into other mediums such as photography, [rug hooking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rug_hooking "Rug hooking"), and wool [dyeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyeing "Dyeing"). Laking held a dual exhibition with Laurie Gunn in [Truro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truro,_Nova_Scotia "Truro, Nova Scotia") in January 2007 consisting entirely of photography.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTERobert_Pope_Foundation201140-18)

In 2013, Laking was the community artist at the White Rabbit Arts Festival in [Upper Economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Economy "Upper Economy") and celebrated 25 years of annual open houses in autumn at the Joy Laking Gallery.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTETruro_Daily_News2013a-19) In 2016, Laking was named [artist-in-residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artist-in-residence "Artist-in-residence") at the [Port Bickerton Lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Bickerton,_Nova_Scotia "Port Bickerton, Nova Scotia").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2016b-20) In 2017, Laking travelled throughout Europe and was given the opportunity to paint in the [gardens of Claude Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fondation_Monet_in_Giverny "Fondation Monet in Giverny").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTECTV_News2017-21) In 2021, Laking's work was featured in two exhibitions at the Fraser Art Gallery in [Tatamagouche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatamagouche "Tatamagouche").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2021-22)

In April 2020, Laking was deeply affected by the [2020 Nova Scotia attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Nova_Scotia_attacks "2020 Nova Scotia attacks"), a mass shooting that began close to her home in [Portapique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portapique "Portapique"). The attacks claimed the lives of 22 people, including three of her friends. The impact of the shootings would affect Laking's career for some time, with her telling [Global News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_News "Global News") in 2021: "After the tragedy, I couldn't see beauty anywhere. (I couldn't paint.) I didn't want to go out in the woods and sit". The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Nova_Scotia "COVID-19 pandemic in Nova Scotia") exacerbated these stressors. She later began spending five hours per day in her studio as a method of coping.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGlobal_News2021-23) On 2 April 2022, nearly two years following the attacks, Laking published a poem on her [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") page titled _Our Portaupique_,[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-25) further reflecting on the changes to the community in the wake of the attacks.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTECTV_News2022Joy_Laking:_''Our_Portaupique''2022-24)

Laking's work is characterized by [representational realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realism_/(arts/) "Realism (arts)"), with a focus on _[plein air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/En_plein_air "En plein air")_ paintings which capture the landscapes of Nova Scotia, particularly in the [Bay of Fundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Fundy "Bay of Fundy") region. She is self-taught in [watercolour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watercolor_painting "Watercolor painting") painting, and is primarily known as a watercolourist; she also uses [oils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_painting "Oil painting") and [acrylics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrylic_paint "Acrylic paint"). Laking's style is influenced by her travels to countries such as India, Ghana, Italy, and Portugal, informing her distinctive portrayals of Nova Scotian scenes.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTESplash_Magazines2022Visual_Arts_Nova_Scotia2014-26) She names [Emily Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Carr "Emily Carr") as inspiration for her work.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2014a-27)

_Invisible Prisons_, a [play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_/(theatre/) "Play (theatre)") by Laking, premiered on 8 March 2013 at the Marigold Cultural Centre in [Truro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truro,_Nova_Scotia "Truro, Nova Scotia"). The play originated from a project in which Laking interviewed 35 victims of [domestic abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_violence "Domestic violence"), creating 14 monologues. The monologues were well-received at a Women's Motivational Luncheon and Laking created the play as a method of further sharing the project. On 17 January 2013, Laking made a presentation to the [Colchester County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colchester_County "Colchester County") Municipal Council requesting financial support in the production of the play. Council voted unanimously to grant her request.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTECouncil_Committee2013-28) The premiere of _Invisible Prisons_ was produced by [Lenore Zann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenore_Zann "Lenore Zann") with a cast from the Truro Theatre Society, with [Bryden MacDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryden_MacDonald "Bryden MacDonald") revising the script and directing the cast.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Shoreline_Journal2013Truro_Daily_News2013b-29) The play has also been performed by the Amherst Comedy Troupe Theatre Group in [Amherst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst,_Nova_Scotia "Amherst, Nova Scotia") in 2014[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2014b-30) and the Osler Society Medicine in Theatre Group at the [Zucker School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zucker_School_of_Medicine "Zucker School of Medicine") in 2020.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZucker_School_of_Medicine2020-31)

In 2019, Laking published her first children's fiction book, _Colours in Winter_. The book was written and illustrated by Laking over 35 years prior to publishing. After sending a copy of the book to [Pottersfield Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottersfield_Press "Pottersfield Press"), a Nova Scotia-based publisher, they agreed to publish it following some alterations to the original work. The 36-page book follows a young girl who expresses disappointment in the lack of colour in the wintertime, wishing for other seasons to come. Colourful [snowflakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake "Snowflake") begin to fall, at first to the delight of the girl, before she begins to feel there is now an overabundance of colour. When the snowflakes return to normal, the girl begins to notice the various colours in nature around her, such as [rose hips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_hip "Rose hip"), birds, and [evergreens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen "Evergreen").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Laking#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPNI_Atlantic_News2019-32)

9.title: QSBOb3ZhIFNjb3RpYSBwYWludGVyIG9uIGhvdyBzaGXigJlzIGNyZWF0aW5nIGEgY2FudmFzIHRvIGNvcGUgYWZ0ZXIgdGhlIG1hc3Mgc2hvb3Rpbmc=
9.content:
Sitting in the bay window of her home in Bass River, N.S., [Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking](http://www.joylakinggallery.com/) painted all morning on April 19, 2020, not knowing that three of her friends were killed the night before.

![Image 1](https://d21y75miwcfqoq.cloudfront.net/70c8fc80)She painted, as she always did, to showcase the spontaneous beauty she saw around her.

But the tragedy of the mass shooting tore through that vision of joy, and the brush suddenly felt too heavy to hold.

“After the tragedy, I couldn’t see beauty anywhere. (I couldn’t paint.) I didn’t want to go out in the woods and sit,” Laking said as she shook her head.

She wore a black sweater featuring the most famous painting by Vincent Van Gogh, _The Starry Night,_ which he painted in 1889 when he was suffering from depression.

Story continues below advertisement

[Blue dominates the painting, blending hills into the sky](https://www.vangoghgallery.com/painting/starry-night.html), which stands in sharp contrast with Laking’s bright and richly coloured paintings that decorate her walls.

Laking has been painting Nova Scotia’s natural landscapes and towns for 44 years, and to her, all of her paintings “sing.”

But a dark shift away from the bright light took place inside of her when Laking first found out that her friend, Lisa McCully, was shot dead.

On April 18, 2020, McCully was one of [22 people killed](https://globalnews.ca/tag/Nova-Scotia-Shooting/) by a gunman dressed as an RCMP officer, who terrorized the province during a 13-hour rampage across rural Nova Scotia.

McCully was a 49-year-old schoolteacher and was killed in her own home.

To Laking, McCully was a “lovely person” who came to every open house at Joy Laking Gallery with her children.

Four days later, Laking got the news that two of her other friends, Joanne Thomas, 58, who grew up in Winnipeg, and her husband, John Zahl, 69, were also shot dead.

_“_They were relatively new to our area and they were just really fantastic people,” Laking said.

Story continues below advertisement

The couple’s house, which was burned to the ground, was one of 16 crime scenes that were being investigated as part of the tragic series of events.

Artist Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking has been painting as a way to cope with her depression. Alexa MacLean/Global News

“I’m not doing well. I’m just still devastated. I have never really had a serious depression, but I sure do now,” she said.

![Image 2: Get the day's top news, political, economic, and current affairs headlines, delivered to your inbox once a day.](https://globalnews.ca/wp-content/themes/shaw-globalnews/images/skyline/national.jpg)

Get daily National news
-----------------------

Get the day's top news, political, economic, and current affairs headlines, delivered to your inbox once a day.

Laking’s personal story is one of three that will be told by Global News in the coming days to show how people living in the community are healing almost a year after the tragic shooting.

Through her art, Laking has found a way to cope. She could rely on her imagination, watercolours and paper to soothe her wounds, although she knows that’s not enough for her to heal from what happened.

“Our biggest problem here, and I realize that most of Nova Scotia do not have family doctors… I have an incredible psychiatrist and therapist…but we don’t have any continuity of care,” said Laking, feeling frustrated and having to look away to compose herself.

Story continues below advertisement

Laking has been married to a retired lawyer for 14 years and has a son and daughter whom she continues to see.

She explained that Dalhousie University in Halifax would bring doctors and medical students to the area to have a “collaborative practice,” but that only happened sporadically.

“I’ve seen three different ones. It’s a whole different thing when you’re seeing somebody that doesn’t know your history.”

This is why “art is everything … what kept me alive,” said Laking.

She would go to the studio five hours every day to cope and remember the victims amid the beautiful colours she uses for her paintings.

![Image 3: Click to play video: 'Support being offered for Nova Scotia’s impacted by mass shooting'](https://i2.wp.com/media.globalnews.ca/videostatic/news/tlvf5r6jf-zjfpmcgihm/web_FREE_SUPPORT_NS_SHOOTING_DRAUS_.jpg?w=1040&quality=70&strip=all)

1:43 Support being offered for Nova Scotia’s impacted by mass shooting

Trending Now

*   [![Image 4](https://globalnews.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/97886d45ae615613a5b467acdd02b0ea5d6b4b2eebb14e306f942d967a947b67.jpg?quality=65&strip=all&w=336&h=224&crop=1) Public servants to learn about job cuts in January](https://globalnews.ca/news/11586819/canada-public-servants-job-cuts/)
*   [![Image 5](https://globalnews.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/c840248d48c61735c4a9aa072ffed900bfddfd0d0ca5767411bd9d72cab689aa.jpg?quality=65&strip=all&w=336&h=224&crop=1) At least 16 files have disappeared from the DOJ webpage for documents related to Jeffrey Epstein](https://globalnews.ca/news/11586484/at-least-16-files-have-disappeared-from-the-doj-webpage-for-documents-related-to-jeffrey-epstein/)

Laking has also contacted McCully’s family saying that she’s prepared to offer her children art classes if they ever wanted to in the hopes that it might help.

Story continues below advertisement

She understands that being surrounded by friends and loved ones during tough times is valuable for one’s healing, but that wasn’t possible due to the [COVID-19](https://globalnews.ca/tag/covid/) pandemic last year and even now.

“COVID-19 added onto the pressure… You can’t get together with friends, you can’t give people a hug, and you can’t even hug your children.”

As someone who has asthma and muscular dystrophy, Laking is also trying to be very careful and not go out much, which also made her feel disconnected from the rest of the community.

“It’s our whole shore that should be pulling together as a community because, like, this, Portapique, is a place name, and it used to be a community, but now with no school, no church, no store… it doesn’t have the cohesiveness now,” she said.

On top of that, Laking said people in the community are “desperate for medical care.”

“We need somebody that we can rely on and that will be there next week and the week after,” she said.

In the wake of the upcoming first anniversary of the mass shooting, Laking said she can’t help but think of the community’s children.

Story continues below advertisement

“All the kids in the school, they might not have lost their moms and dads, and especially the kids who did. I mean, this is huge… and we’re all just kind of dealing with it our own way… and I don’t know if it’ll ever be any good.”

In the meantime, Laking said she’s looking forward to the inquiry into the mass shooting that will be taking place.

The commission of inquiry, formally known as the mass casualty commission, will begin its work investigating how the attack took place and whether there’s anything that could have been done to prevent it.

But before it does, the commission has been accepting applications from potential participants from March until early April. Some people have already been granted permission to participate, including surviving victims and the families of the victims.

“I think when we knew that there were weapons and that there was domestic violence that was reported to police, but it was not taken seriously… This just gives me goosebumps thinking about it. I really hope that by looking at the whole thing, this will never happen again,” said Laking.
